analysis.one_liner: Repeals the Affordable Care Act and its companion law entirely.
analysis.headline: A one-sentence bill to repeal the ACA got no cosponsors, was referred to the Senate Finance Committee, and never received any committee action or vote before the 112th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: S. 16 would erase the Affordable Care Act and the health law passed alongside it in 2010, restoring the law as it stood before they were enacted. It offered no replacement for the ACA's provisions. It was introduced by Senator Vitter with no cosponsors and died in the Senate Finance Committee without a hearing, a vote, or any other action.
analysis.who_benefits: Higher-income households and companies that owed ACA-related taxes and fees would benefit, since the bill repeals the ACA's revenue provisions with nothing to replace them. Anyone who preferred the pre-2010 insurance rules — no requirement that insurers cover pre-existing conditions, no individual mandate — would return to the old system. Millions of people who had gained coverage through the ACA's Medicaid expansion, subsidized private plans, or protections for pre-existing conditions would lose those arrangements.
analysis.who_benefits_short: High earners and firms owing ACA taxes

how_it_helps.text: The bill repeals the Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act and the Health Care and Education Reconciliation Act of 2010 in their entirety and restores prior law as if the ACA had never been enacted.
Because the repeal is total and the bill contains no replacement, every ACA provision — its taxes and fees as well as its coverage rules — would disappear at once.

analysis.who_pays: People who had gained coverage or protections under the ACA — those with pre-existing conditions, young adults on a parent's plan, people getting subsidized coverage or Medicaid — would bear the cost of losing them, and the bill offers no alternative arrangement.
analysis.who_pays_short: People relying on ACA coverage protections

drawbacks.text: The bill repeals the entire ACA with no replacement, so every coverage provision it contains would end at once, alongside the taxes the ACA raised to pay for them.
Restoring prior law 'as if such Acts had never been enacted' would put the health system back to the pre-2010 status quo, with no transition plan for anyone relying on ACA coverage.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For those who believed the ACA was overreach, total repeal had the appeal of simplicity. But the bill's design gave no thought to transition: it would have taken away coverage provisions and consumer protections that millions were using, while returning the money that had been raised for them to the high-income households and industries that paid the ACA's taxes. It read as a statement of opposition rather than a workable plan.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced with no cosponsors, sent to the Senate Finance Committee, and the committee never took it up — no hearing, no vote, nothing — and it died there when the Congress ended in January 2013.

narrative.text: Senator Vitter introduced the bill on January 25, 2011, the opening weeks of the 112th Congress.
No senator signed on as a cosponsor — the bill's cosponsor list stayed at zero for its entire life.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, and the action history shows no further action of any kind before the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: People covered by ACA protections kept them; the industries and high-income households that would have benefited from full repeal got nothing, since the bill never moved.

for.role: U.S. Senator from Louisiana; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on January 25, 2011, and did not attract a single cosponsor in two years.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee

against.what_they_did: Referred the bill on January 25, 2011, and never scheduled a hearing or markup; the bill died in committee.

against.name: Sen. Max Baucus
against.what_they_did: As committee chair, never brought the bill to a markup or hearing during the two-year Congress.

sides.party_line_note: It was a single Republican sponsor with zero cosponsors from either party, so support never extended beyond one senator.

industries.note: Repealing the ACA would have erased the taxes it placed on higher earners, including the Medicare payroll surtax and the tax on investment income. That gain would come directly out of the same bill that ended the ACA's coverage provisions for ordinary people. (These tax provisions are general knowledge about how the ACA was financed, not detailed in the bill text.)

Repeal would have removed the ACA's rate rules and coverage mandates, letting insurers return to practices like denying pre-existing conditions, but it would also have ended the individual mandate and subsidies that steered millions of paying customers to them. The pre-2010 system this bill restores was one in which insurers could decline or price out sick customers. (Mechanism is general knowledge about how the ACA operated.)

The ACA placed annual fees on these industries to help pay for coverage expansion; this bill repeals those fees with the rest of the law, while also ending the expanded coverage that offset some of the cost to them. (Mechanism is general knowledge about ACA financing.)

industries.industry: Healthcare providers serving newly insured patients
industries.note: Hospitals and providers that had counted on the ACA's expansion of coverage would have lost those newly insured patients, and some had accepted lower Medicare payments on that expectation. Repeal would have restored the earlier payment rates while taking away the coverage expansion that paid for them. (Mechanism is general knowledge about ACA financing.)
